title: BM 1200 - Annexure - Stress Testing Guidelines
text:
Guidelines on Stress Testing 
 
           for Commercial Banks 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
Table of Contents 
1. Introduction .................................................................................................................................................... 1 
2. Definition .......................................................................................................................................................... 1 
3. Objectives of Stress Testing ......................................................................................................................... 2 
4. Principles Governing Stress Testing ........................................................................................................... 2 
5. Stress Testing Scope and Coverage ........................................................................................................ 3 
6. Stress Testing Framework ............................................................................................................................. 3 
Annex I: Illustrative List for Sensitivity Tests ................................................................................................. 11 
Annex II: Illustrative List for Scenario Analysis ........................................................................................... 14 
 
 
 
 

1 
 
1. Introduction 
I. 
Stress testing has become an integral part of a bank’s risk 
management system and is used to evaluate its potential 
vulnerability to certain unlikely but plausible events or movements 
in financial variables. The vulnerability is usually measured with 
reference to the bank’s profitability, liquidity and/or capital 
adequacy. Stress testing helps in managing banks' risks by alerting 
bank management and supervisors to the potential impact of 
adverse shocks that are both unexpected and plausible, as well 
as by indicating the necessary financial resources to absorb any 
resulting losses. Thus, stress testing can be a vital tool in identifying, 
monitoring, and assessing risks.  
II. 
These guidelines for stress testing are based on the principles of 
stress testing as outlined in the "Stress testing principles" publication 
by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS). The 
Guideline provides high-level principles that banks should follow 
to establish a reliable Stress Testing Framework.  
2. Definition 
Stress testing consists of the following characteristics: 
I. 
It is carried out by banks using their own internally developed 
models. 
II. 
It relies on assumptions or scenarios provided by the supervisory 
authority or formulated by the bank, which may be subject to 
conservative constraints imposed by authorities. 
III. 
It is established on the bank's internal data and may include a 
high level of data granularity. External data may also be 
incorporated to provide supplementary information. 
IV. 
It pertains to specific portfolios or the bank as a whole, and 
generates comprehensive outcomes regarding the potential 
effects of exposure concentrations, linkages within the bank, and 
contagion probabilities on the bank's loss rates. 
 

2 
 
3. Objectives of Stress Testing 
 
Stress testing is intended to: 
 
I. 
Provide rigorous and forward-looking assessments of risk , as well 
as assist in devising plans to mitigate or prepare for those risks in 
various demanding situations. 
II. 
Aid in the planning process for capital and liquidity and provide 
guidance when undertaking new business activities, entering new 
markets, or undertaking strtageic intiatives. 
III. 
Provide information that will assist in establishing the risk tolerance 
limits of banks. 
4. Principles Governing Stress Testing 
 
I. 
In the course of developing and implementing their stress testing 
activities, banks are required to comply with a series of essential 
principles that have been established on the basis of the "Stress 
Testing Principles" published by BCBS. 
II. 
Banks’ risk management framework must incorporate stress 
testing as a crucial element. Stress testing should aid in identifying 
and controlling risks while also offering a complementary risk 
perspective to other risk management tools. 
III. 
Stress testing should be conducted following the banks' 
applicable 
internal 
policies 
and 
procedures, 
and 
clear 
responsibilities and adequate resources (such as skilled human 
resources and information technology systems) should be 
assigned and allocated to ensure the effective execution of the 
stress tests. 
IV. 
Banks should take the outcomes of the stress tests into account, in 
particular with regard to identified limitations, vulnerabilities and 
shortcomings detected, when setting the institutions strategy and 
when making all relevant decisions affecting capital, liquidity and 
recovery planning. 

3 
 
V. 
For stress tests to be a valuable component of an bank’s risk 
management system, they should be conducted with an 
appropriate frequency. This frequency should be established 
based on the scope and type of the stress test, as well as the 
nature, scale, size, and complexity of the institution (in 
accordance with the principle of proportionality), portfolio 
characteristics, 
and 
changes 
in 
the 
macroeconomic 
environment or the bank's business activities, while adhering to 
the minimum regulatory requirements. 
5. Stress Testing Scope and Coverage 
 
I. 
These Stress Testing Guidelines shall apply to banks on both 
standalone (so1o) level as well as on the consolidated ("Group") 
level.  
II. 
It's important for stress tests to account for all forms of significant 
risk, including on- and off-balance-sheet assets and liabilities. 
Banks should perform stress tests on both the individual portfolio 
and institutional level, covering all types of risk using sensitivity and 
scenario analyses. Banks should also identify risk factors and 
determine the appropriate stress levels for each individual 
portfolio, whenever possible. 
III. 
In order to be effective, stress test scenarios must take into 
account the occurrence of multiple events, rather than assuming 
that events happen independently. Additionally, the scenarios 
should be designed to include a narrative that incorporates 
various events capable of triggering the bank's failure. 
6. Stress Testing Framework  
 
The stress testing framework (STF) of a bank must meet the following 
fundamental requirements: 
 
I. 
General Requirements 
II. 
Involvement and supervision of the board of directors and senior 
management. 
III. 
principal risk factors;  

4 
 
IV. 
stress testing methodologies and scenario selection;  
V. 
data and appropriate Management Information Systems (MIS); 
VI. 
reporting and interpretation of stress test results;  
VII. 
frequency of stress testing; 
VIII. internal controls and independent assessment;  
IX. 
remedial actions. 
 
I. 
General Requirements 
 
a. All banks are required to create and implement a comprehensive 
and well-documented STF that is appropriate for their operations 
and risk profile, and adheres to prudential standards. 
 
b. The STF should cover significant and pertinent risks that are identified 
through a robust identification process, and subject these risks to 
stresses that are appropriately severe. 
 
c. Banks should thoroughly describe and document: the risk 
identification process, the scenarios derived from it, the reasoning 
behind including or excluding identified risks, as well as the 
methodology employed to evaluate the impact of risks. 
 
II. 
The Board of Directors and Senior Management Oversight 
 
a) The Board of Directors is responsible for ensuring that the bank has 
developed and implemented a STF that is approved by the Board, 
appropriate for the bank's unique needs, and integrated into its risk 
management systems. 
 
b) The Board of should ensure that senior management performs their duties 
effectively and sufficiently to develop and implement the bank's STF 
successfully. 
 
c) The Board is also responsible for exercising efficient oversight over the 
bank's stress testing activities and conducting periodic reviews of the 
effectiveness and strength of the STF, at least annually. 

5 
 
 
 
d) The Board shall establish formal lines of authority and the appropriate 
segregation of duties to maintain an effective check and balance within 
the stress testing process. 
 
e) The Board shall establish appropriate stress tolerance limits and shall 
ensure that the appropriate remedial actions that banks may consider 
necessary to address the alarms of stress testing are put in place at 
required point of time. 
 
f) The successful implementation of STF is the responsibility of senior 
management, and it includes: 
 
i. 
Identification of principal risk factors; 
ii. 
Designing and implementing suitable single or multi-factor stress 
tests as part of the STF. 
iii. 
Designing a suitable management information system (MIS) to 
support the stress tests to be conducted as part of the STF. 
iv. 
Ensure to have an appropriate and effective internal control 
mechanism in place to implement and validate stress tests and their 
findings. 
v. 
Review the results of stress tests and monitor for loss limits to ensure 
effective risk management. 
vi. 
Take appropriate remedial actions when necessary to manage risks 
effectively. 
vii. 
Report the stress test results and any actions taken, if any, to the 
Board of Directors on a regular basis. 
viii. 
Ensuring that the staff involved in the stress testing have sufficient 
training and qualifications. 
 
III. 
Principal Risk Factors  
 
a) A bank must identify the critical risks that are subject to stress tests, 
along with their exposures and any correlations between these 
risks. 
b) Banks shall identify the risks to which they are exposed to with regard 
to their bank specific circumstances and portfolios. A suggested list 
of risks that banks in general are exposed to are; credit and 
counterparty risk, credit concentration risk, interest rate risk, equity 
risk, foreign currency risk, liquidity risk, operational risk and country 
risk. These are only anindicative list and banks shall identify the risks 

6 
 
to which they are exposed to with regard to their bank specific 
circumstances and portfolios. 
c) Suggested list of items that a bank shall consider  when designing 
its STF:  
i. 
on and off-balance sheet activities;  
ii. 
business strategy; 
iii. 
portfolio composition; 
iv. 
asset quality; 
v. 
bank-specific events; 
vi. 
operating environment;macro-economic factors (interest 
rate, foreign exchange rate, inflation, GDP growth, asset 
prices, property price index); 
vii. 
historical events; 
viii. 
latest development in the economic, political, geographical 
and global conditions and perspectives. 
 
IV. 
Stress Testing Methodologies and Scenario Selection 
 
A bank's stress events and scenarios must be realistic, appropriate, and 
severe enough to capture the potential risks for its portfolio. The scenarios 
should include a variety of forward-looking, quantitative, and qualitative 
factors, and, if feasible, consider system-wide interactions and feedback 
effects. The STF should include at two or more scenarios, one representing 
a baseline scenario and one or more severe stress scenarios. Besides the 
scenarios provided by the authority, banks may use their own scenarios. 
 
a) The level of complexity of the stress testing models should be 
appropriate for the goals of the exercise and the type and 
significance of the risk being assessed. 
 
b) There are two main categories of stress tests that can be applied to 
a bank: sensitivity analysis and scenarios. These tests can be used 
either independently or in combination with each other. 
 
c) A sensitivity analysis estimates the impact of a single risk factor or a 
small number of closely-related risk factors (e.g. interest rates, FX 
rates, real estate price, equity price etc.) on asset value, asset 

7 
 
quality, earnings, capital or liquidity ratios. In most cases, sensitivity 
tests involve changing inputs or parameters without relating those 
changes to an underlying event or real-world outcome. While it is 
helpful to draw on extreme values from historical periods of stress, 
sensitivity tests should also include hypothetical extreme values to 
ensure that a wide range of possibilities are included. (An illustrative 
list of risk factors is provided in Annex I). 
 
d) Scenario tests involve evaluating the impact on the bank's financial 
position of multiple variables changing simultaneously due to a past 
event or a plausible future event. The bank should identify the 
different risks that will be included in a scenario, consider the 
interconnections among these risks, and evaluate the extent to 
which the stress would affect their financial position. (An illustrative 
list of stress test scenarios is provided in Annex II).  
 
e) The bank should establish effective, significant, and reliable 
methods for converting risk factors into internal risk parameters such 
as probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD), write-offs, fair 
value haircuts, and so on, which provide the bank's perspective on 
risks. 
 
f) The correlation between stressed risk factors and the risk parameters 
should be based not only on the bank's historical experience and 
analysis, but also, where possible and relevant, on benchmarks from 
external sources. 
 
g) Stress testing should be performed over appropriate time horizon to 
effectively capture the risk attributes of exposures, conditions that 
may emerge in the near term, and adverse situations that require a 
longer time to develop. 
h) Assumptions for stress testing: 
 
i. 
Banks should determine various assumptions underlying the 
stress tests and the rationale behind these assumptions. 
 
ii. 
The assumptions selected by banks for the stress tests should 
be well-documented and accessible for review by supervisors 
and auditors. 
 

8 
 
iii. 
The assumptions underlying the stress tests must be reviewed 
periodically to assess their validity, and any changes made 
must be supported by appropriate reasons. Banks must re-
conduct stress tests when there are significant modifications to 
the underlying assumptions. 
 
 
V. 
Data and Appropriate MIS  
 
a) A bank must utilize suitable, precise, and comprehensive data when 
conducting stress tests. 
 
b) Bank should have an adequate data infrastructure which can 
collect, retrieve, process and report the information used in stress 
tests. 
 
c) A bank should establish a sufficiently robust data infrastructure that 
can handle different and possibly evolving stress tests at an 
appropriate level of details.  
 
VI. 
Reporting and Interpretation of Stress Test Results 
 
a) Banks shall be cognizant that the stress tests only indicate the likely 
impact and not the likelihood of the occurrence of the stress events. 
 
b) The effectiveness of stress tests is influenced by the judgment and 
experience of bank, and is therefore contingent upon their ability to 
identify their major risks, correctly understand and interpret the stress 
test results, and take the necessary measures to address the 
situation revealed by the stress test outcomes. 
 
c) The senior management is responsible for reviewing the stress testing 
outcomes and presenting them to the Board for review. 
 
d)  A bank should incorporate the stress testing results into the bank's 
risk management systems. 
 
VII. 
Frequency of Stress Testing 
 
a) The appropriate frequency will depend on several factors including 
the objectives of the stress testing framework, the scope of the stress 
test, the size and complexity of the bank or banking sector, 

9 
 
associated costs, or regulatory requirements as well as changes in 
the macroeconomic environment .  
 
b) Solvency stress tests should be undertaken at least on annual 
frequency. However, banks should conduct stress testing exercises 
more frequently in times of stress and, subsequent to or in 
anticipation of material events. Liquidity stress tests should be 
conducted on a quarterly or higher frequency. 
 
VIII. 
Internal Controls and Independent Assessment  
 
a) The implementation and validation of stress tests and their results 
require an appropriate and effective internal control mechanism. 
 
b) To ensure the quality and effectiveness of stress testing, the bank 
should conduct regular and independent evaluations of its stress 
testing policies, procedures, and processes as part of its internal 
control system. 
 
c) The independent assessment can be conducted by either the 
internal audit team or individuals who are not involved in model 
development or decision-making based on the model output. 
 
IX. 
Remedial Actions 
 
A bank may need to take remedial actions when stress tolerance levels 
are exceeded. These actions may include but are not limited to: 
 
a) Reduction of risk limits; 
 
b) Mitigating risks by increasing collateral requirements and pursuing 
more effective risk mitigation measures. 
c)  Reducing exposures to particular sectors, portfolios, countries, or 
regions as a way to reduce risks 
 
d) Review their pricing and other policies to account for increased 
risks or risks that were not previously identified. This could involve 
adjusting pricing or policy terms to better reflect the level of risk. 
 

10 
 
e) Increase capital levels to strengthen their ability to absorb shocks, 
providing an additional buffer against potential risks. 
f) Implementation of contingency plans; 
 
g) Improve the sources of funds by utilizing credit lines, adjusting their 
liability structure, or modifying their liquid asset profile. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

11 
 
Annex I: Illustrative List for Sensitivity Tests 
 
     Credit and counterparty credit risk 
 
• 
Increases in non-performing loans (‘NPL’) and provisioning levels 
– this assesses the resilience of a bank’s loan portfolios in terms of 
the impact of such increases on its profitability and capital 
adequacy. In designing the scenario, the bank may apply 
different percentages of increase in classified loans and 
provisioning levels to its loan portfolios. 
• 
Rating migration of counterparties – a test based on the internal 
or external credit ratings of bank’s credit exposures, by migrating 
a certain percentage of the credit exposures of a specific rating 
grade (by one or more notches) to a lower rating grade, and 
assessing the resultant impact on a bank’s profitability and capital 
adequacy. The capital impact may include the effects of 
increases in credit losses and provisioning needs, as well as the 
application of higher risk weights due to rating downgrades in the 
calculation of regulatory capital. 
• 
Default of major counterparties – this estimates the impact of 
default of a bank’s major counterparties, including corporate, 
sovereign and bank counterparties, on its profitability, as well as 
liquidity and capital adequacy. The test can be extended to 
cover aggregate exposures to major industries, market sectors, 
countries and regions.  
• 
Decline in the real estate market – this estimates the impact of a 
decline in property prices on collateral coverage, default risk and 
provisioning need for loans secured by properties. 
• 
Decline in the value and market liquidity of financial collateral – 
this estimates the impact of a decline in the valuation and market 
liquidity of financial collateral, which reduces the quality and 
quantity of the collateral, leading to lower collateral coverage 
and recovery rates and higher provisioning needs and capital 
charges. 
 

12 
 
 
     Interest Rate Risk in Banking Book 
 
• 
Gap risk - arises from the term structure of banking book 
instruments, and describes the risk arising from the timing of 
instruments’ rate changes. The extent of gap risk depends on 
whether changes to the term structure of interest rates occur 
consistently across the yield curve (parallel risk) or differentially by 
period (non-parallel risk). 
• 
Basis risk - describes the impact of relative changes in interest rates 
for financial instruments that have similar tenors but are priced 
using different interest rate indices. 
• 
Option risk - arises from option derivative positions or from optional 
elements embedded in the bank’s assets, liabilities and off-
balance sheet items, where the bank or its customer can alter the 
level and timing of their cash flows. Option risk can be further 
characterized into automatic option risk and behavioral option 
risk. 
     Market Risk 
 
• 
Increased volatility in key financial markets assesses the effects of 
increased volatility and adverse movements of market risk factors 
(i.e. interest rates, foreign exchange rates and equity or 
commodity prices) on a bank’s market risk exposures. 
• 
Effect of key monetary decisions by the Central Bank of Oman, 
which might impact stock prices, FX rates and interest rates. 
• 
Effect on the bank arising from a rating downgrade of sovereign, 
leading to widening of credit spreads and a fall in equity prices. 
     Liquidity Risk 
 
• 
Tightening of credit lines - the potential impact of liquidity stress 
on the solvency position arising from a higher cost of funding due 
to tightening of wholesale and deposit/funding markets, and loss 
in the value of marketable securities due to market illiquidity. 

13 
 
• 
Funding concentration – this assesses the liquidity risk of significant 
business activities and concentration to a particular source of 
funding, such as large depositors/funding providers, investment 
account holders, wholesale market funding or holdings of a 
particular asset class. 
• 
Withdrawal risk of investment account holders (‘IAH’)/deposit 
outflows – this assesses the liquidity risk arising from honoring 
redemptions by investment account holders of unrestricted 
investment accounts at the level of individual funds in case of 
Islamic windows. 
 
     Other risks 
 
• 
Decline in net interest income – this estimates the impact on the 
bank’s net interest income due to negative loan growth or 
squeezes in pricing caused by competition for new business or 
market share. 
• 
Risk concentrations – this estimates the impact from changes in 
market conditions which could give rise to risk concentrations. 
Banks may identify and assess the impact of heightened 
correlations or hidden inter-dependencies within and across risk 
types/risk factors, and possible second-round effects under 
severe market shocks that may lead to an increase in bank’s 
exposures. 
• 
Operational risk events – this assesses the effects, on a bank’s 
capital requirement for operational risk, or its ability to maintain 
critical operations and earning capabilities, of external events 
(e.g. external fraud, vendor failure, utility outage and service 
disruption) or internal events (e.g. internal fraud, business 
disruption or system failures, telecommunication problems and 
loss of key personnel).  
 
 
 

14 
 
Annex II: Illustrative List for Scenario Analysis 
 
• Significant  decline in hydrocarbon prices over long horizon (1-3 years) 
that leads to sharp contraction in nominal gross domestic product and 
government public spending. This severe stress scenario would impact the 
banks’ profitability and capitalization through the following risk factor 
chennels:  
 
I. 
Deterioration of corporate borrower balance sheets that resulting 
credit losses on corporate loans which should be assumed to be 
higher than the bassline forecast. (Credit risk) 
 
II. 
Increase in the unemployment rate and high job losses. (Credit risk) 
 
III. 
Declines in aggregate house and real estate prices. (Market risk) 
 
IV. 
Decline in market value of financial instruments due to adverse 
changes in market prices. (Market risk) 
 
V. 
Parallel shifts in the interest yield curve (Market risk) 
 
VI. 
Sharp decline in equity prices. (Market risk) 
 
VII. 
Deterioration of liquidity conditions due to high funding cost and 
Tightening of credit lines. (liquidity risk)
